hints: Think about why CFCs can survive all the way up to the stratosphere unchanged, what does that tell you about their reactivity down below?
Compare bond strengths, the $\text{C-F}$ bond is one of the strongest single bonds while $\text{C-Cl}$ is much weaker and broken by UV.
Link the weak bond breaking to release of chlorine radicals and then to the catalytic destruction of ozone to see which two statements fit together.
walkthrough:
**Recall why CFCs are so stable**

CFCs were used as refrigerants and aerosols precisely because they are very unreactive. They do not react in the lower atmosphere, so they drift unchanged up to the stratosphere.

Think: relatively chemically inert in the troposphere = statement 3 is true.

**Check which bond UV light breaks**

Ultra-violet light in the stratosphere provides enough energy to break the weaker bond only.

$$\text{CCl}_2\text{F}_2 \xrightarrow{UV} \text{ } \dot{\text{C}}\text{ClF}_2 + \text{Cl}\cdot$$

The $\text{C-Cl}$ bond dissociates to give a chlorine radical, but the very strong $\text{C-F}$ bond does not break readily. So statement 1 is false.

**Link chlorine radicals to ozone loss**

The $\text{Cl}\cdot$ radical then catalytically destroys ozone, and is regenerated:

$$\text{Cl}\cdot + \text{O}_3 \rightarrow \text{ClO}\cdot + \text{O}_2$$

This chain reaction is the cause of ozone depletion. So statement 2 is true.

**Combine the true statements**

True statements are 2 and 3 only, while 1 is incorrect. That combination matches the correct option.

options.A: Incorrect. This would mean 1, 2 and 3 are all correct. Statements 2 and 3 are correct, but statement 1 is wrong because only the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond is broken by UV, the $\text{C-F}$ bond is far too strong.
options.B: Incorrect. This would mean 1 and 2 only are correct. Statement 2 is correct, but statement 1 is false and statement 3 is missed out. CFCs are famous for being chemically inert in the troposphere, which is why they reach the stratosphere.
options.C: Correct. Statements 2 and 3 only are correct. CFCs are relatively inert so they survive to the stratosphere, where UV breaks $\text{C-Cl}$ (not $\text{C-F}$) to release $\text{Cl}\cdot$ radicals that deplete ozone.
options.D: Incorrect. This would mean only statement 1 is correct. Statement 1 is actually the false one, since $\text{C-F}$ bonds are not readily dissociated by UV light due to their high bond energy.
